column2: Given these definitions: (1) To face something is to turn toward it rather than away from it, whether for a moment or as a standing. (2) To remain turned away from something is to hold a turning from it, rather than toward it, as a standing over time, and not to be in the course of turning back. (3) To stand turned toward something is to hold a turning toward it as a standing over time, which persists without continuous attention to it. (4) The contrary of a standing is a standing that cannot hold together with it in the same subject, toward the same object, at the same time, though both can be absent. (5) To hold a work as one's own is to acknowledge oneself as its author inwardly and, wherever one speaks of it, in speech as well, neither disowning it nor laying it on another in either. (6) Acknowledging a work of one's own is holding it as one's own and naming it for what it is. (7) A deed is rightly called for by a work of one's own only if it can rightly be done and responds, in proportion, to what the work has done or may yet do, for good or for ill. Then standing turned toward a work of one's own, in acknowledgment and in the deeds it rightly calls for, is the contrary of remaining turned away from that work.
